analysis.one_liner: Bars dominant app stores from forcing developers onto their payment systems or blocking rival app stores.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2025 with bipartisan sponsorship and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no vote or further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets the two companies that control nearly all app distribution on smartphones in the United States. It would stop them from forcing app makers to use their built-in payment systems, from punishing developers who offer cheaper prices elsewhere, and from blocking users from installing rival app stores. It also stops the platform owner from copying features of other companies' apps using data collected from its store, and lets developers sue for triple damages if they are harmed.
analysis.who_benefits: App developers, especially smaller ones, who keep more of their sales instead of paying the platform's cut, and consumers, who benefit when developers can offer cheaper payment options and the platforms can no longer bury competing apps in search results.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small app developers and app buyers

how_it_helps.text: Covered companies can no longer require developers to use their own in-app payment system as a condition of distribution, opening the door to cheaper payment options.
Users gain the right to install third-party apps and app stores, set defaults, and delete preinstalled apps from the platform owner.
The platform owner cannot use nonpublic data collected from other companies' apps to build competing products, and cannot rank its own apps ahead of rivals in search results.
Developers harmed by violations can sue in federal court for threefold damages plus attorney's fees, and state attorneys general and the FTC can enforce the law.

analysis.who_pays: Apple and Google, which own the two dominant app stores and collect a commission on most in-app sales, would lose a major revenue stream; consumers could face some added risk if app review is loosened, though the bill contains security and privacy exceptions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Apple and Google's app store commissions

drawbacks.text: Critics, including Apple, argue that allowing apps to be installed outside the official store and enabling rival app stores would expose users to more malware, scams, and privacy risks; the bill responds with security and fraud exceptions, but whether those hold up would depend on court tests.

The bill does not directly cap app store commissions, so any savings for developers and consumers depend on competition actually materializing, and the platform owners can still defend restrictive practices by proving in court that they are necessary for privacy, security, or antifraud purposes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real: app store commissions run up to 30% on in-app purchases, and loosening that grip could lower prices for digital goods and let smaller developers keep more revenue. The main honest cost is security risk from loosened distribution controls, which the bill tries to manage through narrow exceptions but cannot fully eliminate. On balance this is a competition bill with clear consumer upside and a manageable, though real, downside.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the record shows no committee vote or other action since.

narrative.text: Senator Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on June 24, 2025, joined by four senators from both parties: Richard Blumenthal, Mike Lee, Amy Klobuchar, and Dick Durbin.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced.
No further action appears in the record: no committee vote, no floor action, and no additional cosponsors beyond the original five are listed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, Apple and Google. While the bill sits without action, they keep collecting commissions on app sales that the bill would subject to competition, and nothing has changed for developers or consumers.

for.name: Marsha Blackburn
for.role: U.S. Senator from Tennessee, lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Apple
against.role: Operator of the iPhone App Store and iOS, the bill's largest covered company
against.what_they_did: Opposed the similar prior version of this bill, arguing it would weaken app security and privacy, and campaigned against it.

against.name: Google
against.role: Operator of the Google Play Store and Android, the other main covered company
against.what_they_did: Opposed the similar prior version of this bill and lobbied against it.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, has taken no action on it; the record shows only the referral with no committee vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican and drew five cosponsors split evenly between the parties (3 of 45 Senate Democrats and 2 of 55 Senate Republicans), so support does not follow party lines.

industries.industry: Apple and Google (mobile operating systems and app stores)
industries.note: The two companies collect commissions of up to 30% on most in-app purchases because they are the only practical way to reach smartphone users. The bill would force their payment systems and stores to compete, which is exactly the revenue at stake.

Developers would keep more of their revenue by choosing payment providers and would gain the right to sue for triple damages. Their interest in lower platform fees runs directly alongside consumers' interest in lower prices.

industries.industry: Alternative payment processors and third-party app stores
industries.note: The bill creates space for rival payment systems and app stores to operate on iOS and Android, which the current rules largely block.

analysis.trajectory: The bill's prospects look poor. A nearly identical version in a previous Congress cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee in 2022 but never received a Senate floor vote. With no committee action scheduled and only original cosponsors so far, the most likely path is that the bill stays in the Judiciary Committee without a vote unless its sponsors push for a markup and build a larger cosponsor list.
